sentences.text: This animal possessed a robust skeleton featuring a deep, narrow-fronted skull that widened significantly toward the back.
Its jaws held dagger-like teeth designed for tearing flesh.
The creature reached an estimated length of five to six meters, making it one of the largest carnivorous reptiles of its time.
The pelvis included a hooked pubis and a rod-like ischium, structures similar to those found in carnosaurs.
Forelimbs were roughly sixty-four percent the size of the hind limbs, ending in small hands with five toes and a single claw on the first digit.
A complete skeleton was recovered from a quarry in New Mexico between 1988 and 1989.
Well-preserved remains of a specific species revealed previously unknown anatomical parts of the genus.
One specimen represents the largest rauisuchian reptile recovered from that specific quarry and the first articulated example found in eastern North America.
The genus was formally established by Chatterjee in 1985.
The name means "Post crocodile" and refers to the Post Quarry in Texas where the type species fossils were found.
In 1980, paleontologists at Texas Tech University discovered a fossil-rich site near Post, Texas, yielding a dozen specimens of a new rauisuchid.
Specimens similar to this animal were discovered in Crosby County, Texas, in 1920 and described by Ermine Cowles Case in 1922.
It served as an apex predator in the Triassic, larger than small contemporary dinosaurs like Coelophysis.
This hunter fed on large herbivores such as dicynodonts and preyed on upland creatures like Placerias.
It also consumed other herbivores like Trilophosaurus and Typothorax.
Tooth replacement differed from modern crocodiles, as new teeth grew until old ones were fully resorbed rather than fitting directly into pulp cavities.
The function of the single claw on the first digit is uncertain, though it may have aided in grappling prey.
It lived in a tropical, moist, and warm environment containing ferns, gymnosperms, and cycads.
The animal inhabited highlands alongside Coelophysis and other archosaurs such as Desmatosuchus and Typothorax.
This genus belongs to the clade Pseudosuchia, the lineage of archosaurs that includes modern crocodilians, and includes two species: P. kirkpatricki and P. alisonae.
Many juvenile skeletons originally assigned to P. kirkpatricki were reclassified by Long and Murry as a distinct genus named Chatterjeea elegans.
Postosuchus lived in North America during the Late Triassic, specifically the Norian to Rhaetian stages, approximately 221 to 203 million years ago.
Historically, scientists debated whether rauisuchids like Postosuchus were primarily bipedal or quadrupedal, with no consensus among scientists.
In 2002, David J. Gower argued that a braincase assigned to Postosuchus was incomplete and might actually belong to an ornithodire.
